name: Bone marrow / bone broth

card.summary: Slow-simmered bones and marrow, promoted for collagen and skin; popular as a food, with no published trials on appearance.
card.note: Reference sources state there is no scientific evidence for many of the health claims made for bone broth.

quick.overview:
Bone broth is stock made by simmering bones and connective tissue in water for a long time, and bone marrow is the fatty tissue inside long bones, eaten roasted or in soups. In wellness and looksmaxxing circles both are promoted for collagen, skin, joints and gut health.

Bone broth became a wellness trend in the early 2010s. Wikipedia reports there is no scientific evidence to support many of the claims made for it, and no published trial was found testing it for skin or appearance.
quick.mechanism: Simmering releases collagen from bones and connective tissue, which turns into gelatin. Proponents say eating this collagen supports skin and joints; how dietary collagen or gelatin is digested and whether it reaches skin in a meaningful way has not been established for broth specifically.
quick.risks: Broth and marrow are ordinary foods and are generally not regarded as risky for most people. Marrow is high in fat, and bones can concentrate contaminants in some preparations. Vertebral spinal marrow is banned for sale in some countries, including the UK, because of mad cow disease concerns.

lead: Bone broth is a cooking liquid made by simmering bones, often with meat scraps, vegetables and herbs, for an extended period. During simmering, collagen in bones and connective tissue turns into gelatin, which thickens the liquid [1]. Bone marrow is the edible tissue inside long bones, found in yellow and red forms, and has been eaten for a very long time [2].

Health claims about bone broth became popular in the early 2010s, helped by books such as Nourishing Broth (2014), and bone broth bars and delivery services grew in the United States [1]. In looksmaxxing and wellness communities, broth is promoted for collagen, skin and joint support.

Wikipedia states that there is no scientific evidence to support many of the claims made for bone broth, citing NPR and Harvard Health [1]. No published trial was found testing bone broth or marrow consumption for skin quality or appearance.

paras: Stock is a savoury cooking liquid made by simmering bones, meat, seafood or vegetables, and bone broth is another name for bone-based stock. Bones and connective tissue release collagen that becomes gelatin, so bone-based stocks are usually thicker than meat-based broths [1].

Bone marrow is sold in bone-in cuts and is eaten in many cuisines, such as phở in Vietnam, bulalo in the Philippines, nalli nihari in India and Pakistan, and ossobuco in Italy. Red marrow is reported to contain more nutrients than yellow marrow [2].

Some anthropologists think early humans cracked bones to reach marrow, with stone tools used for this going back almost 2 million years, and Neanderthals rendering marrow fat about 125,000 years ago [2]. In 18th century Europe diners used special marrow scoops, and marrow now appears in some restaurant dishes [2].
The modern wellness trend dates from the early 2010s, and a 2019 scene from The Mandalorian in which a character sips broth became an internet meme [1].

Proponents in wellness and ancestral-diet communities say broth supplies collagen, gelatin and minerals that support skin, joints and gut lining. These are the claims behind its appearance as a skin food. Published research on whether ingested broth changes skin has not been identified.

No studies found. No published human trial was found testing bone broth or bone marrow consumption for skin, hair or appearance outcomes. Wikipedia reports that there is no scientific evidence supporting many of the health claims made for bone broth [1].

timeline.event: Health claims for bone broth become popular, followed by broth bars and delivery services in the United States [1].
The book Nourishing Broth helps popularise the health claims [1].
